title: Chemistry formula sheet (symbols, units, conditions, worked examples)
description: 75 formulas for organic and analytical chemistry, from pH, buffers and solubility products, the Nernst equation, Faraday’s law and the Beer–Lambert law to chemical shift, degree of unsaturation, isotope patterns, retention factor and resolution, plate number, integrated rate laws, Arrhenius and Eyring, ΔG° = −RT ln K, the Carothers equation, Bragg and Scherrer, detection limits, uncertainty, atom economy and the E factor, each with symbols and units, conditions of use, common mistakes and a numerical example. Print only the formulas you pick on A4.
lead: The formulas used in organic and analytical chemistry courses, exams and the lab, grouped by topic. Each one lists symbols with units, conditions and range, common mistakes and a numerical example, and the dimensions of both sides have all been checked by machine. Links lead to calculators that use the same formula.
note: Example values are this site’s calculator defaults or match the practice questions and textbooks (sources are given per formula). Some property values, such as standard potentials, pKa values and molar absorption coefficients, are given only for the example. For experiments and reports, check values against the literature or standards.

p: Type a formula name, symbol or term (“Nernst”, “t_R”, “resolution”) in the search box to keep only the matching formulas, or narrow them with the topic buttons. Each heading has a link (#f-…) that jumps straight to that formula.

Tick “Pick” on a formula to add it to your own formula sheet. “Print picked only” prints the formulas and symbol tables of the picked items on A4 in two columns (10–15 formulas fit on one or two pages). Tick “Also print conditions and examples” to include those as well.

“Copy link to picked” gives a URL (?f=…) that opens the same selection. Picks are also kept in this browser (localStorage) and never sent to a server. If your browser blocks storage, the URL still restores them.

guide.h: How dimensions and examples were checked
p: For every formula, a program converted the units in the symbol table to SI base units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol) and confirmed that both sides of each line have equal dimensions and that the arguments of exp, ln and log are dimensionless. Logarithms of concentrations (pH, pK_a, the Nernst equation) are treated as dimensionless quantities divided by the standard concentration c° = 1 mol/L.

All numerical examples were also recalculated by a separate program and matched with the values on this page, using CODATA 2022 constants. For quantities whose units depend on order, such as rate constants, the [ ] shows a representative case (for example first order).

units_lead: Conversions for units common in chemistry, for making units consistent before using a formula (after NIST SP 811 and the SI Brochure, 9th ed.; numbers calculated from CODATA 2022 constants).

units.q: formulas used in SI, e.g. Randles–Ševčík

units.b: c [mol/L] = c [mg/L]/(1000 M [g/mol]) (Cd, 112.41 g/mol: 1.00 mg/L = 8.90 µmol/L)
10⁻⁶ (by mass 1 mg/kg; about 1 mg/L in dilute water)
10⁻⁹ (1 µg/kg; about 1 µg/L in dilute water)

units.q: ΔG° per unit of log₁₀ K

const_lead: CODATA 2022 recommended values (Mohr et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002 (2025); physics.nist.gov/cuu). “Exact” marks constants fixed by the 2019 SI and quantities derived from them. Figures in parentheses are the standard uncertainty in the last digits. The examples use these values (some calculators use rounded values such as R = 8.314).
faq: Should I use activities or concentrations?

The Nernst equation, equilibrium constants and the definition of pH are properly written with activities. Concentrations are fine only for dilute solutions where the ionic strength is low and activity coefficients are about 1. In salty solutions or with di- and trivalent ions the difference grows, so estimate activity coefficients with the Debye–Hückel equation, or use concentration-based equilibrium constants or formal potentials determined at the same ionic strength.
Should I measure peak width at the baseline or at half height?

Either gives the same answer for Gaussian peaks as long as the coefficient matches. With the baseline width W (= 4σ), N = 16(t_R/W)² and R_s = 2Δt_R/(W₁ + W₂). With the half-height width W_{½} (= 2.355σ), N = 5.54(t_R/W_{½})² and R_s = 1.18Δt_R/(W_{½,1} + W_{½,2}). Check which width your data system reports and never mix the coefficients. For tailing peaks the two methods disagree.
Do I divide by n or n − 1 for the standard deviation?

When estimating the spread of a population from a few measurements, as in chemical analysis, divide by n − 1 (sample standard deviation s). Dividing by n underestimates it (by about 11 % for n = 5). Tables for confidence intervals, t tests and Grubbs’ test assume s. Calculators and spreadsheets offer both functions, so check which one you used.
What is the difference between 3σ and 3.3σ/S for the detection limit?

Both convert into concentration the signal, as a multiple of the blank noise, above which the analyte cannot be said to be absent. Analytical chemistry textbooks (Harris and others) often use 3s/S, three times the blank standard deviation divided by the sensitivity; pharmaceutical method validation (ICH Q2(R2), 2023, as in the earlier Q2(R1)) gives 3.3σ/S. How σ is obtained also varies: replicate blanks, residuals of the calibration line, or the standard deviation of the intercept. The quantification limit is usually 10σ/S in both. State the factor and the source of σ when you report.
Why do second-order rate constants for 2A → P differ by a factor of 2 between books?

Because the rate is defined differently. IUPAC defines the rate of reaction as v = −(1/ν)d[A]/dt (ν the stoichiometric coefficient), so for 2A → P, v = −½ d[A]/dt = k[A]². Many books instead define k by the loss of A, −d[A]/dt = k[A]², as do this site’s kinetics calculator and this formula sheet. The two k values differ by a factor of 2, so check the definition before using literature values.
Which formulas use ln and which use log?

The Arrhenius and Eyring equations, ΔG° = −RT ln K, the van ’t Hoff equation and first-order integrated rate laws use the natural log ln. pH, pK_a, absorbance, Henderson–Hasselbalch, the Hammett equation and the 25 °C Nernst equation (0.05916 V) use log₁₀. Since ln x = 2.303 log₁₀ x, a mix-up gives an error of a factor of 2.303.
What is the [ ] to the right of each formula?

The dimensions of both sides of that line in SI base units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol). Potential, for example, is kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻¹ (= V), molar concentration is m⁻³·mol (= mol/m³; 1 mol/L = 10³ mol/m³), and dimensionless quantities show 1. Formulas that use customary units such as mol/L, cm or °C are still checked in SI. Use it to check the unit of your answer.
Can the example values differ slightly from the calculators?

Examples that use the calculator defaults (buffer, Beer–Lambert, chromatography, isotope pattern, kinetics) match what the calculators show. The kinetics calculator uses R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) while this page uses the CODATA value of R, so activation energies differ in the fifth digit (52.946 versus 52.949 kJ/mol). The calculator shows four significant figures, so both appear as 52.95 kJ/mol.

ph.name: pH and pOH
m: standard concentration, 1 mol/L (makes the log argument dimensionless)
ph.when: Aqueous solutions. The concentration form is an approximation for dilute solutions where activity coefficients can be taken as 1 (low ionic strength). pK_w depends on temperature; 14.00 is the value at 25 °C.
ph.miss: Using the natural log ln. Taking the pH of 1.0×10⁻⁸ mol/L HCl as 8 (this ignores the dissociation of water; the real value is about 6.98, still acidic). Using pH + pOH = 14 at temperatures other than 25 °C.
ph.ex: 0.050 mol/L NaOH (25 °C, activity coefficients 1): pOH = −log₁₀ 0.050 = 1.30, so pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.
ph.kw: pH pOH hydrogen ion ion product of water Kw activity

ka.name: Acid dissociation constant Ka and pKa
m: equilibrium concentrations of the weak acid, its conjugate base and H⁺
base dissociation exponent of the conjugate base
exponent of the ion product of water (14.00 at 25 °C)
ka.when: Dilute aqueous solution at constant temperature. The thermodynamic K_a is written with activities and is dimensionless; the concentration form shifts slightly with ionic strength.
ka.miss: Reading the pK_a of 9.25 for ammonia as a property of NH₃ (it is the pK_a of the conjugate acid NH₄⁺; NH₃ has pK_b = 4.75). Thinking a larger pK_a means a stronger acid (it is the opposite).
ka.kw: acid dissociation constant Ka pKa pKb conjugate base

weak-acid.name: pH of a weak acid solution
m: total (formal) concentration of the weak acid
weak-acid.when: When the degree of dissociation is small (about 5 % or less) so that C − [H⁺] ≈ C. If the solution is so dilute that water dissociation matters, or K_a is large, solve the quadratic [H⁺]²/(C − [H⁺]) = K_a.
weak-acid.miss: Dropping the square root ([H⁺] = K_a C). Using pH = pK_a for a plain weak acid solution (it holds only when [HA] = [A⁻]).
weak-acid.ex: 0.10 mol/L acetic acid (K_a = 1.8×10⁻⁵ mol/L): [H⁺] ≈ √(1.8×10⁻⁶) = 1.34×10⁻³ mol/L, pH = 2.87 and α = 1.3 %. Solving the quadratic gives [H⁺] = 1.33×10⁻³ mol/L and pH = 2.88, so the approximation is close.
weak-acid.kw: weak acid pH degree of dissociation acetic acid approximation quadratic

henderson.name: Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
m: acid dissociation exponent of the weak acid
henderson.when: An approximation with activity coefficients of 1 that ignores the change in concentrations from dissociation of the acid itself and of water. It works well for concentrations above about 0.01 mol/L and pH within pK_a ± 1.
henderson.miss: Inverting the ratio ([HA]/[A⁻]). Using ln instead of log. Forgetting that only the ratio matters, so dilution leaves the pH (approximately) unchanged.
henderson.ex: Acetic acid 0.10 mol/L with sodium acetate 0.15 mol/L (pK_a 4.76): pH = 4.76 + log₁₀ 1.5 = 4.94. For pH 5.00 the ratio is 10^{0.24} = 1.74; with a total of 0.10 mol/L that is 0.0635 mol/L sodium acetate and 0.0365 mol/L acetic acid.

fraction.name: Fractions of the acid and base forms
m: fractions of the total present as conjugate base and as acid
fraction.when: Monoprotic acids, with the pH fixed by a buffer and not changed by the dissolved substance. Polyprotic acids need the expressions with stepwise K_a values.
fraction.miss: Forgetting that pH − pK_a = 1 means 90 % and 2 means 99 %, and assuming half-and-half at any pH. For a base (BH⁺/B) the fraction of B corresponds to α(A⁻).
fraction.ex: A weak acid with pK_a 4.76 at pH 7.40: α(HA) = 1/(1 + 10^{2.64}) = 0.0023, so 0.23 % is in the neutral form.
fraction.kw: fraction neutral form ionized form dissociation alpha speciation

buffer-capacity.name: Buffer capacity
m: buffer capacity (strong base per liter needed to change the pH by 1)
buffer-capacity.when: A monoprotic buffer. The contribution of water itself, 2.303([H⁺] + [OH⁻]), is left out (add it in strongly acidic or basic solutions, or for dilute buffers). 0.576 = 2.303/4.
buffer-capacity.miss: Assuming the capacity is the same outside pK_a ± 1. Forgetting that doubling the total concentration at the same ratio leaves the pH unchanged but doubles the capacity.
buffer-capacity.ex: C = 0.10 mol/L: at pH = pK_a, β = 0.0576 mol/L per pH unit. At pH = pK_a ± 1 it is 2.303 × 0.10 × 10/121 = 0.0190 mol/L, 33 % of the maximum.

activity.name: Activity and ionic strength (Debye–Hückel)
l: limiting law; A ≈ 0.509 in water at 25 °C
activity.when: The limiting law only fits very dilute solutions. At higher concentrations use forms that include the ion size, such as the extended Debye–Hückel equation. Strictly the concentrations are molalities (mol/kg), nearly equal to mol/L in dilute water.
activity.miss: Forgetting z² in the ionic strength (a divalent ion counts four times). Taking the salt concentration as the ionic strength (1 mol/L Na₂SO₄ has an ionic strength of 3 mol/L).
activity.kw: activity activity coefficient ionic strength Debye Huckel

titration.name: Titration stoichiometry
titration.when: The reaction goes to completion with the stated stoichiometry and the end point matches the equivalence point (indicator error is estimated separately).
titration.miss: Swapping the coefficients (with 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻, MnO₄⁻ is 2/5 of C₂O₄²⁻). Mixing mL and L. Forgetting the purity and drying of the primary standard used for standardization.
titration.ex: Potassium hydrogen phthalate 0.4084 g (204.22 g/mol) = 2.000×10⁻³ mol needs 20.40 mL of NaOH, so c = 0.09803 mol/L. If 1.000×10⁻³ mol sodium oxalate takes 20.00 mL KMnO₄, MnO₄⁻ is 2/5 of that, 4.000×10⁻⁴ mol, giving 0.02000 mol/L.
titration.kw: titration equivalence point standardization neutralization redox stoichiometry

ksp.name: Solubility product and molar solubility
m: cation and anion concentrations in the saturated solution
ksp.when: Activity coefficients of 1, and ions that do not hydrolyze or form complexes. With a common ion present, include its concentration (solubility drops).
ksp.miss: Comparing salts of different stoichiometry by K_sp alone (Ag₂CrO₄ has a smaller K_sp than AgCl but is more soluble). Forgetting the factor m^{m} x^{x}.
ksp.ex: AgCl (K_sp = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰): s = √(1.8×10⁻¹⁰) = 1.34×10⁻⁵ mol/L. Ag₂CrO₄ (1.1×10⁻¹²): s = (1.1×10⁻¹²/4)^{1/3} = 6.50×10⁻⁵ mol/L, more soluble than AgCl.
ksp.kw: solubility product Ksp solubility precipitation common ion

nernst.name: Nernst equation
m: electrode potential (written for the reduction half-reaction)
nernst.when: A reversible electrode reaction at equilibrium, with essentially no current flowing (potentiometry). Written with concentrations, it is off by the activity coefficients (a formal potential E°′ absorbs this).
nernst.miss: Dropping n (for two electrons the factor halves to 0.0296 V). Inverting Q and getting the sign wrong. Using 0.05916 at temperatures other than 25 °C.
nernst.kw: Nernst electrode potential standard potential reaction quotient

nernst-slope.name: Slope of ion-selective and pH electrodes
m: charge number of the measured ion (opposite sign for anions)
nernst-slope.when: For an electrode with Nernstian response. Real slopes are often slightly below theory, so they are found by calibrating with two or more standards. The slope is proportional to temperature, so temperature compensation is needed.
nernst-slope.miss: Mixing up RT/F (25.7 mV, per natural-log unit) with the slope per decade. Using 59 mV for a divalent ion such as Ca²⁺.
nernst-slope.kw: Nernstian slope ion-selective electrode pH electrode glass electrode calibration 59 mV

dg-e.name: Cell potential, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant
m: electrons transferred per unit of reaction
dg-e.when: Relations between standard-state quantities. With the left electrode of the cell diagram as anode (oxidation) and the right as cathode (reduction), E° = E°(right) − E°(left).
dg-e.miss: Doubling E° when a half-reaction is doubled (E° is intensive and stays the same; ΔG° doubles). Mixing kJ and J in ΔG°.
dg-e.kw: cell potential emf Gibbs energy equilibrium constant standard potential

faraday.name: Faraday’s law of electrolysis
faraday.when: Current efficiency of 100 % (no side reactions). With current efficiency η, multiply m by η. Coulometric titration and coulometry use the same relation.
faraday.miss: Dropping z (2 for Cu²⁺). Mixing mA with A or minutes with seconds.
faraday.kw: Faraday electrolysis charge coulometry current efficiency

randles-sevcik.name: Randles–Ševčík equation (CV peak current)
randles-sevcik.when: A reversible, diffusion-controlled system at a planar electrode with semi-infinite diffusion. At 25 °C in cm-based units, i_p = 2.69×10⁵ n^{3/2} A D^{1/2} C v^{1/2} (A in cm², D in cm²/s, C in mol/cm³). Quasi-reversible and irreversible systems have different coefficients.
randles-sevcik.miss: Putting mol/L into the 2.69×10⁵ form (it needs mol/cm³). Expecting i_p ∝ v (it goes as √v). Forgetting that adsorbed species give i_p ∝ v.
randles-sevcik.ex: n = 1, a 3.0 mm diameter electrode (A = 7.07×10⁻⁶ m²), C = 1.0 mmol/L, taking D = 1.0×10⁻⁹ m²/s, v = 0.100 V/s, 25 °C: i_p = 1.90×10⁻⁵ A = 19.0 µA. Quadrupling v doubles it.
randles-sevcik.kw: Randles Sevcik cyclic voltammetry CV peak current scan rate

beer.name: Beer–Lambert law
beer.when: Monochromatic light, dilute solution (no interactions or association between molecules), negligible scattering and fluorescence. On most instruments the error is smallest for absorbance of about 0.1–1.
beer.miss: Entering the path length in mm (with ε in L/(mol·cm) it must be cm). Putting % transmittance straight into A. Forcing a straight line through a calibration curve bent by high concentration or stray light.
beer.ex: NADH (340 nm, ε = 6220 L/(mol·cm)) in a 1 cm cell with A = 0.45: c = 0.45/6220 = 7.23×10⁻⁵ mol/L = 72.3 µmol/L.
beer.kw: Beer Lambert absorbance molar absorption coefficient path length quantitation

absorbance.name: Absorbance and transmittance
absorbance.when: Absorbance is defined with the decimal log (a “Napierian absorbance” with ln also exists but is rarely used in analytical chemistry). I₀ is measured on a blank with solvent and cell.
absorbance.miss: Taking the log of %T without dividing by 100. Thinking absorbance 2 means twice the absorption (it transmits 1 %, a tenth of the light at absorbance 1).

beer-mix.name: Additivity of absorbance for mixtures
m: molar absorption coefficient of component i at that wavelength
beer-mix.when: Components that do not react or associate and each follow the Beer–Lambert law. For n components, measure at n or more wavelengths and solve the simultaneous equations. Choosing wavelengths where the ε values differ strongly keeps errors small.
beer-mix.miss: Trying to determine two components from a single wavelength. Using ε values that were not measured at the same wavelengths.
beer-mix.ex: l = 1.00 cm, 2000x + 500y = 0.60 at λ₁ and 200x + 1000y = 0.44 at λ₂ (ε in L/(mol·cm)): x = 2.0×10⁻⁴ mol/L and y = 4.0×10⁻⁴ mol/L.
beer-mix.kw: additivity multicomponent simultaneous equations mixture absorbance

wavenumber.name: Wavenumber, wavelength and photon energy
wavenumber.when: Vacuum values. The wavelength in air is shorter by the refractive index (about 1.0003), which routine spectroscopy usually ignores. λ [µm] = 10⁴/ν̃ [cm⁻¹], λ [nm] = 10⁷/ν̃ [cm⁻¹], E [eV] = 1239.84/λ [nm].
wavenumber.miss: Using cm⁻¹ in hcν̃ without converting to m⁻¹ (a factor of 100). Treating wavenumber and frequency as the same thing. Mixing per molecule and per mole (multiply by N_A).
wavenumber.ex: 1715 cm⁻¹ (C=O stretch): λ = 10⁴/1715 = 5.831 µm, E = hcν̃ = 3.407×10⁻²⁰ J = 0.2126 eV, or 20.52 kJ/mol. A 254 nm photon is 4.881 eV.
wavenumber.kw: wavenumber wavelength cm-1 photon energy eV infrared IR

oscillator.name: Harmonic-oscillator vibrational wavenumber
m: reduced mass (multiply values in u by 1.660 54×10⁻²⁷ kg)
oscillator.when: Treats a diatomic (or a bond whose stretch involves essentially two atoms) as a harmonic oscillator. Anharmonicity and coupling to other vibrations shift real molecules slightly.
oscillator.miss: Using the lighter mass instead of the reduced mass. Mixing c in cm/s and m/s. Expecting deuteration to halve the wavenumber (it drops to about 1/√2; from C–H to C–D it is about 1/1.36).
oscillator.ex: C–H at 3000 cm⁻¹ (taking C = 12, H = 1, D = 2): μ(C–H) = 0.923 u and μ(C–D) = 1.714 u, so C–D is at 3000 × √(0.923/1.714) = 2201 cm⁻¹. The force constant is k = (2πcν̃)²μ = 489 N/m.
oscillator.kw: reduced mass force constant stretching vibration isotope deuterium infrared

fl-qy.name: Fluorescence quantum yield (relative method)
m: quantum yields of sample and reference
integrated fluorescence intensities under the same conditions
fl-qy.when: Same excitation wavelength, slits and detection settings; keep absorbance low to avoid inner-filter effects and reabsorption. Valid where intensity is proportional to absorbance (strictly, the ratio of 1 − 10^{−A}).
fl-qy.miss: Inverting the absorbance ratio (more absorbed light means more emission, so divide by A). Forgetting the refractive-index correction with different solvents. Comparing peak heights instead of integrated intensities.
fl-qy.kw: fluorescence quantum yield relative method reference standard refractive index

stern-volmer.name: Stern–Volmer equation (quenching)
m: fluorescence intensity without and with quencher
stern-volmer.when: A straight line when one quenching mechanism (dynamic or static) acts. With both, the plot curves upward. Dynamic quenching also shortens the lifetime (τ₀/τ = F₀/F); static quenching does not change it.
stern-volmer.miss: Dropping the “1 +”. Swapping F/F₀ and F₀/F.
stern-volmer.ex: K_SV = 150 L/mol, [Q] = 0.020 mol/L: F₀/F = 1 + 3.0 = 4.0, so the intensity is 25 %. With τ₀ = 5.0 ns, k_q = 3.0×10¹⁰ L/(mol·s), above the diffusion limit (about 10¹⁰), which points to static quenching.

chem-shift.name: Chemical shift
chem-shift.when: TMS is set to δ = 0. δ does not depend on the magnetic field, whereas the offset in Hz scales with the field and J couplings stay constant in Hz.
chem-shift.miss: Getting the MHz and Hz orders wrong (Hz divided by MHz gives ppm directly). Thinking δ grows at higher field.
chem-shift.ex: 2920 Hz from TMS at 400 MHz: δ = 2920/400 = 7.30 ppm. At 600 MHz the same δ is 4380 Hz.
chem-shift.kw: chemical shift ppm TMS shielding NMR

larmor.name: Larmor frequency
larmor.when: Bare-nucleus value. Nuclei in molecules are shielded by electrons and resonate lower by parts per million (the chemical shift).
larmor.miss: Confusing γ with γ/2π (a factor of 2π). Forgetting that γ differs between nuclei and assuming ¹³C resonates at the ¹H frequency (it is about a quarter).
larmor.ex: ¹H at B₀ = 9.4 T: ν₀ = 42.577 × 9.4 = 400.2 MHz (a “400 MHz instrument”). At 14.1 T it is 600.3 MHz.
larmor.kw: Larmor resonance frequency gyromagnetic ratio magnetic field NMR

multiplicity.name: Multiplicity from spin–spin coupling
m: number of equivalent coupled neighboring nuclei
spin quantum number of those nuclei (1 for ²H)
multiplicity.when: First-order spectra (chemical-shift difference Δν much larger than J) with all neighbors coupled by the same J. For I = ½ the intensities follow Pascal’s triangle.
multiplicity.miss: Counting the proton’s own H. Lumping two sets of neighbors with different J into one (it gives a doublet of doublets). Forgetting that exchange of OH or NH can remove the coupling.
multiplicity.ex: The CH₂ of CH₃CH₂Br has three neighboring H, so 4 lines (1 : 3 : 3 : 1). The ¹³C of CDCl₃ couples to one D (I = 1): 2 × 1 × 1 + 1 = 3 lines (1 : 1 : 1).
multiplicity.kw: n+1 rule spin coupling splitting multiplet Pascal

dbe.name: Degree of unsaturation (rings plus double bonds)
m: numbers of C, H and N atoms
dbe.when: Neutral molecules made of C, H, N, O, S and halogens (O and S are not counted). A triple bond counts 2 and a benzene ring 4.
dbe.miss: Counting O. Forgetting that halogens count like H. Not suspecting an ion (even-electron ion) or a wrong formula when the answer is a half-integer.
dbe.ex: C₈H₈O₂: U = 8 − 4 + 1 = 5 (for example a benzene ring, 4, plus a C=O). C₆H₅Cl: 6 − 2.5 − 0.5 + 1 = 4. C₄H₁₁N: 4 − 5.5 + 0.5 + 1 = 0.
dbe.kw: degree of unsaturation DBE double bond equivalent rings molecular formula

isotope.name: Chlorine and bromine isotope patterns
m: fraction of molecules with k heavy isotopes
number of Cl or Br atoms
light and heavy isotope abundances (³⁵Cl 0.7576, ³⁷Cl 0.2424, ⁷⁹Br 0.5069, ⁸¹Br 0.4931)
isotope.when: Each atom picks its isotope independently, giving a binomial distribution. With both Cl and Br, convolve the two distributions (expand (a + b)ⁿ(c + d)ᵐ). Contributions from ¹³C, ³⁴S and others are not included.
isotope.miss: Swapping the rules (Cl is about 3 : 1, Br about 1 : 1). Expecting the peak at M+1 (the mass difference is 2, so M+2).
isotope.ex: CH₂Cl₂ (two Cl): M : M+2 : M+4 = 100 : 64.0 : 10.2. Br₂: 51.4 : 100 : 48.6 (M+2 is the strongest).
isotope.kw: isotope pattern chlorine bromine M+2 M+4 binomial mass spectrometry

m-plus-1.name: M+1 peak and number of carbons
m: intensity of M+1 relative to M
m-plus-1.when: An estimate from ¹³C alone (about 1.08 % per carbon). ¹⁵N, ²H, oxygen and sulfur add a little. The ¹³C abundance varies slightly between samples.
m-plus-1.miss: Dividing M+1 by the base peak or the total instead of M. Applying it when the molecular ion is weak or overlaps with [M+H]⁺.
m-plus-1.ex: Six carbons (e.g. chlorobenzene): 6 × 1.07/98.93 × 100 = 6.49 %. The “1.1 % × n” rule of thumb gives 6.6 %.
m-plus-1.kw: M+1 carbon count 13C isotope peak mass spectrometry

mass-error.name: Mass error (ppm) and protonated ions
m: measured and calculated (from the formula) values
monoisotopic mass of the neutral molecule
mass-error.when: Confirming elemental formulas by high-resolution MS. Use exact masses of the most abundant isotopes (¹H 1.007 825 03, ¹²C 12, ¹⁴N 14.003 074 00, ¹⁶O 15.994 914 62 u).
mass-error.miss: Adding the hydrogen-atom mass (1.007 825) for [M+H]⁺ (the cation lacks an electron, 0.000 549 u, about 3 ppm near m/z 200). Calculating with average atomic weights (H 1.008 and so on).
mass-error.ex: Caffeine C₈H₁₀N₄O₂: M = 194.080 376, [M+H]⁺ = 195.087 652. A measured 195.0870 is −3.3 ppm. Adding the hydrogen-atom mass instead would give −6.2 ppm.
mass-error.kw: mass error ppm exact mass high resolution protonated ESI monoisotopic

retention-factor.name: Retention factor
m: hold-up time (time for an unretained solute)
retention-factor.when: Constant conditions (isocratic, isothermal) with retention by partitioning between stationary and mobile phases. k is the ratio of time spent in the stationary phase to time in the mobile phase.
retention-factor.miss: Using t_R − t₀ without dividing by t₀. Dividing t_R by t₀ (that is 1 + k). Applying it to gradient chromatograms.
retention-factor.ex: t₀ = 1.50 min, t_R = 6.00 min: k = 4.50/1.50 = 3.00. With the calculator defaults (t₀ 1.0 min, 5.0 and 5.8 min), k₁ = 4.0 and k₂ = 4.8.
retention-factor.kw: retention factor capacity factor retention time hold-up time t0 HPLC GC

selectivity.name: Separation factor (selectivity)
m: retention factors of the earlier and later peaks
selectivity.when: Two adjacent components. α is set by the stationary phase, mobile phase and temperature, not by column length or flow. With α = 1 no number of plates will separate them.
selectivity.miss: Taking the ratio of retention times t_R2/t_R1 as α (it is the ratio of retention factors, after subtracting t₀).
selectivity.ex: k₁ = 4.0, k₂ = 4.8: α = 1.20, not the ratio of retention times 5.8/5.0 = 1.16.

resolution.name: Resolution
m: retention times of the two peaks
baseline widths (between the tangents at the inflection points, = 4σ)
resolution.when: For Gaussian peaks both forms give the same value (1.18 = 2 × 2.355/4). For peaks of similar height, R_s ≥ 1.5 is essentially baseline separation.
resolution.miss: Putting half-height widths into the factor-2 formula (R_s comes out about 1.7 times too large). Mixing minutes and seconds between times and widths.
resolution.ex: Calculator defaults: 2 × (5.8 − 5.0)/(0.40 + 0.44) = 1.90. For 8.0 and 8.6 min with widths of 0.40 min each, 1.5.
resolution.kw: resolution Rs baseline width half height width

plates.name: Plate number
plates.when: Gaussian peaks, isocratic and isothermal. The value differs between components. Tailing peaks give low values (use moments or similar). 8 ln 2 = 5.545; 5.54 is the rounded value.
plates.miss: Using 16 with the half-height width or 5.54 with the baseline width. Subtracting t₀ from t_R (that gives the effective plate number, a different quantity).
plates.kw: plate number theoretical plates column efficiency half height baseline width

hetp.name: Plate height (HETP)
hetp.when: Valid for the conditions under which N was measured (same compound, flow and temperature). Smaller packing particles give smaller H.
hetp.miss: Getting the mm–µm conversion wrong. Thinking a larger H is better (smaller is more efficient).
hetp.ex: L = 150 mm, N = 13 850: H = 0.0108 mm = 10.8 µm. Calculator defaults (N = 2780): 54.0 µm.

purnell.name: Purnell resolution equation
m: retention factor of the later peak
purnell.when: Two adjacent peaks of nearly equal width. It splits resolution into efficiency (N), selectivity (α) and retention (k) to show which change helps most.
purnell.miss: Expecting R_s to double when N doubles (it rises by √2). Mixing up k₁ and k₂. Some textbooks use the average k, which gives slightly different numbers.
purnell.ex: For α = 1.10 and k₂ = 4.0 to reach R_s = 1.5: √N = 4 × 1.5 × 11 × 1.25 = 82.5, so N = 6806 (about 6.8×10³ plates).
purnell.kw: Purnell resolution equation required plates efficiency selectivity retention

van-deemter.name: van Deemter equation
van-deemter.when: An approximation with A, B and C independent of flow. B scales with the diffusion coefficient in the mobile phase, so it is large in GC and small in HPLC.
van-deemter.miss: Mixing volumetric flow (mL/min) with linear velocity (m/s). Thinking higher u is always better (the C term raises H).
van-deemter.ex: Taking A = 5.0 µm, B = 4.0×10⁻⁹ m²/s and C = 4.0×10⁻³ s: u_opt = √(10⁻⁶) = 1.0 mm/s and H_min = 5.0 + 2 × 4.0 = 13 µm.
van-deemter.kw: van Deemter linear velocity optimum flow eddy diffusion mass transfer

rf.name: Rf value (thin-layer chromatography)
m: distance from origin to the center of the spot
distance from origin to the solvent front
rf.when: Same plate, same eluent and a saturated chamber. It changes with plate activity, humidity and temperature, so run standards on the same plate.
rf.miss: Measuring from the bottom edge of the plate (measure from the origin). Measuring to the leading edge of the spot (use the center).
rf.ex: Origin 1.0 cm from the bottom, solvent front at 8.5 cm, spot at 4.0 cm: R_f = 3.0/7.5 = 0.40.

kovats.name: Kováts retention index
m: carbon number of the earlier bracketing n-alkane
adjusted retention times t_R − t₀ (analyte and bracketing n-alkanes)
kovats.when: Isothermal GC with the analyte eluting between two n-alkanes. For temperature-programmed runs use the linear form without logarithms (van den Dool–Kratz).
kovats.miss: Taking logs without subtracting t₀. Comparing temperature-programmed indices directly with isothermal ones.
kovats.ex: t₀ = 1.00 min, C8 at 5.00 min, C9 at 9.00 min, analyte at 6.66 min: I = 100 × [8 + (log 5.66 − log 4.00)/(log 8.00 − log 4.00)] = 850.

internal-std.name: Internal standard method
m: peak areas of analyte and internal standard
concentrations of analyte and internal standard (same units)
internal-std.when: Detector response proportional to concentration, an internal standard absent from the sample and eluting near but separated from the analyte. It cancels variations in injection volume and preparation losses.
internal-std.miss: Treating the area ratio as the concentration ratio (skipping F). Not using the right c_S when the internal-standard level differs between sample and standards.
internal-std.ex: A standard (X 10.0 mg/L, internal standard 20.0 mg/L) with an area ratio of 0.600 gives F = 1.20. A sample (internal standard 20.0 mg/L) with ratio 0.900 gives c_X = 0.900 × 20.0/1.20 = 15.0 mg/L.
internal-std.kw: internal standard response factor relative response peak area ratio

rate-law.name: Integrated rate laws (zero, first, second order)
m: concentration of A at time t and initially
rate constant (zero order mol/(L·s), first s⁻¹, second L/(mol·s))
rate-law.when: Rate defined as −d[A]/dt = k[A]ⁿ, constant temperature, no reverse or side reactions. Second order means 2A → P, or A + B → P with equal initial concentrations. With B in large excess, A decays pseudo-first-order (k′ = k[B]₀).
rate-law.miss: Using a k defined with the IUPAC rate v = −½ d[A]/dt for 2A → P in −d[A]/dt = k[A]² (they differ by a factor of 2). Running the zero-order law past [A] = 0.
rate-law.ex: First order, [A]₀ = 0.10 mol/L, k = 2.0×10⁻³ s⁻¹, t = 600 s: [A] = 0.10 e^{−1.2} = 0.0301 mol/L, 69.9 % reacted. Second order, [A]₀ = 0.20 mol/L, k = 0.050 L/(mol·s), t = 100 s: [A] = 0.10 mol/L.
rate-law.kw: rate law integrated first order second order zero order pseudo-first-order rate constant

half-life.name: Half-life and time for 90 % reaction
half-life.when: From the integrated forms of −d[A]/dt = k[A]ⁿ. Only first order is independent of initial concentration. For second order t₉₀ = 9/(k[A]₀); for zero order 0.9[A]₀/k.
half-life.miss: Using ln 2/k for every order. Forgetting that second-order half-lives lengthen as the reaction proceeds.

arrhenius.name: Arrhenius equation
m: rate constants (any order, compared in the same units)
arrhenius.when: Over a range where E_a and A can be taken as temperature-independent. A plot of ln k against 1/T has slope −E_a/R.
arrhenius.miss: Entering temperatures in °C. Using log₁₀ instead of ln (a factor of 2.303). Mixing kJ and J in E_a.
arrhenius.ex: Rate doubles from 25 °C to 35 °C (298.15 K → 308.15 K): E_a = 8.3145 × 0.6931/1.0884×10⁻⁴ = 52.95 kJ/mol (the calculator, with R = 8.314, gets 52.946 kJ/mol and also shows 52.95 kJ/mol).
arrhenius.kw: Arrhenius activation energy pre-exponential factor temperature dependence

eyring.name: Eyring equation (transition-state theory)
m: Gibbs energy and enthalpy of activation
eyring.when: For bimolecular reactions with k in concentration units, the right side gains (c°)⁻¹ and ΔG‡ refers to the standard concentration (1 mol/L). A plot of ln(k/T) against 1/T has slope −ΔH‡/R.
eyring.miss: Using log₁₀ instead of ln. Treating E_a and ΔH‡ as equal (they differ by RT ≈ 2.5 kJ/mol). Reading a large negative ΔS‡ only as “slow” (it indicates an associative, ordered transition state).
eyring.kw: Eyring transition state theory Gibbs energy of activation enthalpy entropy of activation

hammett.name: Hammett equation
m: rate constants with substituent X and unsubstituted (same units)
reaction constant (electronic demand of the reaction)
substituent constant (σ_m, σ_p; defined from benzoic acid ionization)
hammett.when: Meta and para substituents on a benzene ring. Ortho substituents fall off because of steric effects. Reactions with direct resonance interaction use σ⁺ or σ⁻. The same form applies to equilibrium constants (log(K_X/K_H) = ρσ).
hammett.miss: Reversing the meaning of the sign of ρ (ρ > 0 means negative charge builds up in the transition state, so electron-withdrawing groups accelerate). Using ln instead of log₁₀.
hammett.ex: ρ = +2.50 and p-NO₂ (σ_p = 0.78): log₁₀(k_X/k_H) = 1.95, so 89 times faster.
hammett.kw: Hammett substituent constant reaction constant sigma rho linear free-energy relationship

kie.name: Kinetic isotope effect (zero-point energy)
m: ratio of rate constants for H and D substrates
Planck constant, speed of light, Boltzmann constant
kie.when: An upper estimate for a primary isotope effect, assuming the stretch is completely lost in the transition state and only zero-point energy matters. Tunneling can push values higher.
kie.miss: Dropping the ½ in the zero-point energy ½hcν̃ (squaring the result). Not converting cm⁻¹ to m⁻¹ (hc/k_B = 1.4388 cm·K is convenient).
kie.kw: kinetic isotope effect KIE deuterium zero-point energy kH/kD

gibbs-k.name: Standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant
gibbs-k.when: K refers to standard states (c° = 1 mol/L in solution, p° = 1 bar for gases). It also gives conformer and isomer populations, and product ratios (with ΔΔG‡, same form, under kinetic control).
gibbs-k.miss: Mixing ln and log (ΔG° = −2.303RT log₁₀ K; at 25 °C, 2.303RT = 5.708 kJ/mol). Taking the log of a K that still carries units (L/mol, etc.).
gibbs-k.ex: Methylcyclohexane, equatorial more stable by 7.3 kJ/mol, 25 °C: K = e^{7300/(8.3145 × 298.15)} = 19.0, so 95.0 % equatorial.
gibbs-k.kw: Gibbs energy equilibrium constant ΔG RT lnK population conformer

gibbs.name: Gibbs energy, enthalpy and entropy
gibbs.when: Constant temperature and pressure. Where ΔH and ΔS change little with temperature, the direction of spontaneity switches at T = ΔH/ΔS, where ΔG = 0.
gibbs.miss: Subtracting ΔS in J from ΔH in kJ (a factor of 1000). Entering °C.
gibbs.ex: Association constant K = 1.0×10⁵ L/mol (referred to c°), ΔH° = −40.0 kJ/mol, 25 °C: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −28.5 kJ/mol, so TΔS° = ΔH° − ΔG° = −11.5 kJ/mol (enthalpy-driven).
gibbs.kw: Gibbs enthalpy entropy spontaneity ΔG ΔH ΔS

vant-hoff.name: van ’t Hoff equation (temperature dependence of K)
m: equilibrium constants at T₁ and T₂
vant-hoff.when: Over a range where ΔH° is roughly constant. A plot of ln K against 1/T has slope −ΔH°/R.
vant-hoff.miss: Expecting K to rise with temperature for an exothermic reaction (ΔH° < 0; it falls). Reversing the order in 1/T₂ − 1/T₁.
vant-hoff.ex: ΔH° = −20 kJ/mol and K = 10 at 25 °C: at 50 °C, ln(K₂/10) = −0.624, so K₂ = 5.36.
vant-hoff.kw: van t Hoff equilibrium constant temperature reaction enthalpy

mn-mw.name: Number- and weight-average molar mass, dispersity
m: amount of chains with molar mass M_i
mn-mw.when: Definitions valid for any distribution. M_w ≥ M_n, equal only for a monodisperse sample. Osmometry and end-group analysis give M_n, light scattering gives M_w. GPC often gives values relative to polystyrene standards.
mn-mw.miss: Taking the mass-weighted mean Σw_iM_i/Σw_i as M_n (it is M_w). Mixing masses and amounts in the averages.
mn-mw.kw: number-average weight-average molar mass dispersity PDI polydispersity Mn Mw

carothers.name: Carothers equation
m: extent of reaction (of the minority group)
carothers.when: Step-growth polymerization of bifunctional monomers, without cyclization or side reactions and with reactivity independent of chain length.
carothers.miss: Taking X_n directly as the number of repeat units (in AA–BB polymers two structural units make one repeat unit). Taking r as majority/minority.
carothers.ex: p = 0.99: X_n = 100. With r = 0.98 and p = 0.99: X_n = 1.98/(1.98 − 1.9404) = 50.0, halved by a small imbalance.
carothers.kw: Carothers degree of polymerization step-growth polycondensation extent of reaction

flory-dist.name: Most-probable distribution in step growth (Flory)
m: weight- and number-average degree of polymerization
flory-dist.when: Linear step growth with equal reactivity and stoichiometric balance (Flory’s most-probable distribution). As p → 1, Đ → 2.
flory-dist.miss: Applying 2 to chain-growth polymers (termination mode changes it, e.g. 1.5–2).
flory-dist.kw: most probable distribution Flory dispersity step growth

ceiling.name: Ceiling temperature
ceiling.when: ΔH_p and ΔS°_p independent of temperature. Above T_c long chains do not form. Lower monomer concentration lowers T_c.
ceiling.miss: Dividing kJ by J. Losing a sign and getting a negative temperature. Not checking which standard state (1 mol/L or neat monomer) the ΔS° refers to.
ceiling.ex: ΔH_p = −35.0 kJ/mol, ΔS°_p = −104 J/(mol·K): T_c = 336.5 K (63.4 °C). At [M] = 0.10 mol/L it falls to 284.2 K.
ceiling.kw: ceiling temperature depolymerization enthalpy of polymerization entropy

mayo-lewis.name: Copolymer composition (Mayo–Lewis)
m: mole fraction of M₁ in the copolymer formed
mole fractions of monomers in the feed (f₁ + f₂ = 1)
reactivity ratios r₁ = k₁₁/k₁₂, r₂ = k₂₂/k₂₁
mayo-lewis.when: Terminal model (reactivity set only by the last unit of the growing chain), at low conversion while the feed composition is unchanged.
mayo-lewis.miss: Assuming F₁ equals the feed composition. Reading r₁ ≈ r₂ ≈ 0 as “does not copolymerize” (each chain end adds the other monomer, giving an alternating copolymer).
mayo-lewis.kw: copolymerization Mayo Lewis reactivity ratio copolymer composition

living.name: Degree of polymerization in living polymerization
m: initial monomer and initiator concentrations (or amounts)
molar mass of the monomer unit
combined molar mass of the end groups
living.when: No termination or chain transfer, initiation much faster than propagation, and each initiator starting one chain (a bifunctional initiator gives one chain growing at both ends). The distribution is narrow and Đ is close to 1.
living.miss: Forgetting initiator efficiency or deactivation by impurities. Ignoring end groups when comparing (they matter for short chains).
living.ex: 1.00 mmol sec-butyllithium fully polymerizing 10.4 g styrene (0.100 mol, 104 g/mol): X_n = 100, M_n = 100 × 104 + 58 = 1.05×10⁴ g/mol (end groups sec-butyl 57 and H 1).
living.kw: living polymerization anionic initiator degree of polymerization molar mass control

bragg.name: Bragg’s law
m: Bragg angle (between beam and planes; diffractometers read 2θ)
bragg.when: The diffraction condition, treating the planes as mirrors. Higher orders are usually treated as first order from planes with spacing d/n.
bragg.miss: Using 2θ as θ. Mixing degrees and radians.

cubic-d.name: Interplanar spacing in cubic crystals
cubic-d.when: Cubic crystals only. Extinction rules: fcc shows only reflections with h, k, l all odd or all even; bcc only those with h + k + l even (diamond structure has extra restrictions).
cubic-d.miss: Using it for tetragonal or hexagonal crystals. Dropping the square root.
cubic-d.ex: From Si(111) with d = 0.313 58 nm (the Bragg example), a = 0.313 58 × √3 = 0.5431 nm. For Cu(111) with d = 0.2087 nm, a = 0.3615 nm.
cubic-d.kw: interplanar spacing lattice parameter Miller indices cubic extinction

scherrer.name: Scherrer equation (crystallite size)
m: line broadening from crystallite size (FWHM in radians, instrument broadening removed)
scherrer.when: Crystallites below roughly 100 nm with little strain broadening (separate strain with a Williamson–Hall plot or similar). It gives the size of coherently diffracting domains, not the particle size.
scherrer.miss: Using β in degrees. Mixing up the 2θ width and θ (β is the width measured in 2θ). Not subtracting instrumental broadening.
scherrer.kw: Scherrer crystallite size line broadening FWHM XRD

xps.name: XPS binding energy
m: binding energy (relative to the Fermi level)
X-ray energy (Al Kα 1486.6 eV, Mg Kα 1253.6 eV)
measured kinetic energy of the photoelectron
xps.when: Conductive samples in electrical contact with the spectrometer. Insulators charge and shift, so correct with C 1s (e.g. 284.8 eV) and state the reference used.
xps.miss: Using the sample’s work function (it is the spectrometer’s). Reading kinetic energy as binding energy.
xps.kw: XPS binding energy photoelectron work function kinetic energy ESCA

imfp.name: XPS sampling depth (inelastic mean free path)
m: fraction of signal from depths up to z
emission angle from the surface normal
imfp.when: Composition uniform with depth, elastic scattering ignored. λ depends on electron kinetic energy and material; for XPS it is a few nm.
imfp.miss: Measuring the angle from the surface instead of the normal. Taking λ itself as the sampling depth (λ gives 63 %; 95 % needs 3λ).
imfp.ex: λ = 2.0 nm, normal emission: 1 − e^{−3} = 0.950, so 95 % comes from the top 6.0 nm. At 45°, 4.24 nm.
imfp.kw: sampling depth inelastic mean free path IMFP angle-resolved XPS surface sensitivity

dsc-xc.name: Crystallinity from DSC
m: enthalpy of cold crystallization during heating
enthalpy of melting of 100 % crystalline polymer (literature value)
dsc-xc.when: A heating scan. Subtracting cold crystallization gives the crystallinity before the measurement. Literature ΔH°_m values vary, so state the one used. For composites, divide by the polymer mass fraction.
dsc-xc.miss: Forgetting to subtract cold crystallization. Mixing J/g and J/mol (per repeat unit).
dsc-xc.ex: PET with ΔH_cc = 20.0 J/g, ΔH_m = 50.0 J/g and taking ΔH°_m = 140 J/g: X_c = 30.0/140 = 21.4 %.
dsc-xc.kw: crystallinity DSC differential scanning calorimetry enthalpy of melting cold crystallization

mean-sd.name: Mean, standard deviation and RSD
m: relative standard deviation (%, same as CV)
mean-sd.when: Divide by n − 1 (degrees of freedom) when estimating the population standard deviation from a finite sample. Divide by n only for a complete population.
mean-sd.miss: Using the calculator’s σ key (divides by n). Forgetting to express RSD in %. Confusing the standard deviation with the standard error of the mean s/√n.
mean-sd.kw: mean standard deviation relative standard deviation RSD CV coefficient of variation n-1 repeatability

ci.name: Confidence interval of the mean
m: population mean (estimate of the true value)
t value for n − 1 degrees of freedom (two-sided, at the chosen level)
ci.when: Normally distributed results without systematic error. The interval covers random error only, not bias.
ci.miss: Using t for n instead of n − 1 degrees of freedom. Forgetting to divide by √n. Using a one-sided t value.
ci.kw: confidence interval t distribution standard error 95% degrees of freedom

t-test.name: t test (mean versus a reference value)
m: t statistic (compared with the critical t)
t-test.when: Normally distributed results. If t exceeds the critical value for n − 1 degrees of freedom, the difference is significant (bias). Comparing two means needs a different formula depending on whether variances are equal.
t-test.miss: Reading “not significant” as “no difference” (it only cannot be detected with this n). Mixing one- and two-sided critical values.
t-test.ex: Certified 50.0 mg/kg, five results with x̄ = 51.2 and s = 1.0: t = 1.2 × √5/1.0 = 2.68, below the two-sided 5 % critical value for 4 degrees of freedom (2.776), so the difference is not significant.
t-test.kw: t test significance certified reference material bias trueness

lod-loq.name: Limit of detection and limit of quantification
m: standard deviation of the blank signal (or low-level samples, or regression residuals; absorbance in the example)
lod-loq.when: A calibration line that stays linear at low concentration, with normally distributed blank noise. The factors (3, 3.3, 10) and the way σ is taken (blank, residuals, intercept) differ by guideline and field, so state the convention. Here the signal is divided by the slope to give a concentration.
lod-loq.miss: Mixing the LOD in signal (blank mean + 3s) with the LOD in concentration (3s/S). Reporting values near the LOD as quantitative results (quantify above the LOQ).
lod-loq.kw: limit of detection LOD limit of quantification LOQ 3 sigma 3.3 sigma 10 sigma blank sensitivity

recovery.name: Spike recovery
recovery.when: When the added analyte is extracted and measured like the native analyte (spikes may not bind to the matrix like native analyte, which can make recovery look high).
recovery.miss: Dividing the spiked result by (native + added) instead of subtracting the native amount.
recovery.ex: Unspiked 2.0 mg/kg, 6.5 mg/kg after adding 5.0 mg/kg: R = (6.5 − 2.0)/5.0 × 100 = 90 % (6.5/7.0 = 93 % is wrong).

uncertainty.name: Combined and expanded uncertainty
m: combined standard uncertainty of the result y
relative standard uncertainty of each input
coverage factor (2 for about 95 % with a normal distribution)
uncertainty.when: When y is a product or quotient of uncorrelated inputs (for sums and differences, add absolute uncertainties in quadrature). In general, multiply by sensitivity coefficients ∂f/∂x_i and add in quadrature (GUM).
uncertainty.miss: Adding uncertainties linearly. Mixing relative and absolute values. Reporting an expanded uncertainty without stating k.
uncertainty.kw: measurement uncertainty combined standard uncertainty expanded uncertainty coverage factor GUM propagation

std-addition.name: Standard addition
m: analyte concentration in the sample solution
signal before and after the addition (e.g. absorbance)
concentration and volume of the standard added
std-addition.when: Signal proportional to concentration (through the origin) and the same matrix effect for sample and spike. Subtract the blank signal first. In practice, several additions and the x-intercept of the line are more reliable.
std-addition.miss: Dividing by A₂ (divide by the difference A₂ − A₁). Forgetting the dilution of the sample by the standard’s volume.
std-addition.ex: A₁ = 0.200, and A₂ = 0.450 after a spike raising the concentration by 2.0 mg/L: c_x = 2.0 × 0.200/0.250 = 1.6 mg/L. With 0.100 mL of 200 mg/L added to 10.0 mL of sample and the same signals, c_x = 1.57 mg/L.
std-addition.kw: standard addition matrix effect spike extrapolation atomic absorption

extraction.name: Solvent extraction (repeated)
m: fraction remaining in water after n extractions
volumes of water and of organic solvent per extraction
extraction.when: D independent of concentration, equilibrium reached each time and clean phase separation.
extraction.miss: Confusing D with the partition coefficient K_D (D is what changes with pH). Multiplying the first extraction by n.
extraction.ex: D = 4.0, 100 mL water extracted four times with 25 mL: q = (100/200)⁴ = 0.0625, so 93.75 % extracted. One 100 mL extraction gives 80 %.
extraction.kw: solvent extraction distribution ratio repeated extraction liquid-liquid extraction

distribution.name: Distribution ratio and pH
m: partition coefficient of the neutral form
hydrogen-ion concentration in the aqueous phase
distribution.when: The ionic form does not enter the organic phase, and there is no association or complexation. Drug log D at pH 7.4 uses the same idea.
distribution.miss: Using the acid formula for a base (a base extracts better at higher pH). Confusing K_D with D.
distribution.ex: To extract a base B (pK_a of BH⁺ 9.0) at 99 % of K_D or more, [H⁺] ≤ K_a/99, i.e. pH ≥ 9.0 + log₁₀ 99 = 11.0.
distribution.kw: distribution ratio partition coefficient pH logD logP extraction ionization

yield.name: Yield
m: mol of product per mol of limiting reagent (ratio of coefficients)
yield.when: Based on the limiting reagent (the one smallest after dividing by its coefficient). Use purity-corrected amounts.
yield.miss: Basing it on an excess reagent. Dividing masses directly (compare amounts when molar masses differ). Thinking 100 % yield means no waste (atom economy is separate).
yield.ex: 12.0 g of product (150.2 g/mol) from 0.100 mol of limiting reagent: 0.0799 mol, a 79.9 % yield.
yield.kw: yield limiting reagent theoretical yield isolated yield

ee.name: Enantiomeric excess
m: specific rotations of the sample and of the pure enantiomer
ee.when: Estimating ee from optical purity requires specific rotation proportional to ee (non-linear effects break it). Accurate ee comes from chiral HPLC or GC, or NMR.
ee.miss: Taking ee as the major fraction (80 : 20 is 60 % ee). Mixing ee and de (diastereomeric excess).
ee.ex: R 80.0 %, S 20.0 %: ee = 60.0 %. If the pure R enantiomer is −50.0°, the specific rotation is −30.0°. At 75 % ee the major enantiomer is (100 + 75)/2 = 87.5 %.
ee.kw: enantiomeric excess ee enantiomer optical purity asymmetric synthesis

specific-rotation.name: Specific rotation
l: l in dm, c in g/mL
m: specific rotation (customarily written in degrees; strictly deg·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹)
specific-rotation.when: Report the wavelength λ (e.g. the sodium D line), temperature T, solvent and concentration. Specific rotation varies with solvent and concentration.
specific-rotation.miss: Using l in cm or c in g/100 mL (factors of 10 and 100). Confusing observed rotation with specific rotation.
specific-rotation.kw: specific rotation optical rotation polarimeter sodium D line chiral

atom-economy.name: Atom economy
m: molar mass of the desired product (times its coefficient)
molar mass of reactant i (times its coefficient)
atom-economy.when: A theoretical value set by the equation alone (no yield, solvent or work-up). Catalysts are not counted. For multistep routes, include the reactants of all steps.
atom-economy.miss: Counting by-products as product and getting 100 %. Forgetting coefficients. Treating it as the same as yield.
atom-economy.kw: atom economy atom efficiency green chemistry

e-factor.name: E factor and process mass intensity
l: when E includes all water and solvent
m: E factor (kg waste per kg product)
process mass intensity (kg input per kg product)
masses of waste, total input and product
e-factor.when: Conventions for E differ on whether water is included and how recycled solvent is counted, so state the scope. PMI counts all reactants, reagents, solvents and water (as used in the pharmaceutical industry).
e-factor.miss: Counting recovered and reused solvent as waste (subtract what is recovered). Treating E and PMI as the same number (PMI is one larger).
e-factor.ex: Product 50 kg, raw materials and reagents 120 kg, solvent 900 kg (80 % recovered), water excluded: waste 70 + 180 = 250 kg, so E = 5.0. Product 5.0 kg from 30 kg reactants and reagents, 400 kg solvent and 170 kg water: PMI = 600/5.0 = 120.
e-factor.kw: E factor PMI process mass intensity waste green chemistry

rme.name: Reaction mass efficiency (RME)
m: total mass of reactants actually used (including excess)
rme.when: Combines atom economy, yield and reagent excess in one number. Solvents, catalysts and work-up materials are usually excluded.
rme.miss: Using stoichiometric amounts (count the excess actually charged). Confusing it with atom economy.
rme.ex: Acetic acid 6.00 g (0.100 mol) and ethanol 9.20 g (0.200 mol, twofold) giving 7.04 g of ethyl acetate: RME = 7.04/15.20 × 100 = 46.3 %. Counting only the stoichiometric 4.60 g of ethanol would give 66.4 %, ignoring the excess.
rme.kw: reaction mass efficiency RME mass efficiency green chemistry

adiabatic.name: Adiabatic temperature rise
m: maximum temperature of the synthesis reaction
fraction of unreacted reagent accumulated at the time of failure
adiabatic.when: No heat loss (adiabatic) and c_p independent of temperature. The vessel’s heat capacity is not included (including it lowers the value slightly). Compare MTSR with decomposition onset and boiling point to rate the risk.
adiabatic.miss: Mixing kJ and J or kg and g. Forgetting that in semi-batch only the accumulated fraction counts.
adiabatic.ex: Δ_rH = −120 kJ/mol, 1.5 mol per kg, c_p = 1.8 kJ/(kg·K): ΔT_ad = 120 × 1.5/1.8 = 100 K. Running at 60 °C with 35 % accumulated gives MTSR = 60 + 35 = 95 °C.
